Scandinavian Tobacco Group (STG-DK) · Triaging A&J Memo, 24-Nov-26

Scandinavian Tobacco Group: a 13% earnings yield that is about to be paid out again, if 2027 profit holds without the 2026 refunds

Share price DKK 85.4 on 23-Nov-26. Money figures are in Danish kroner (DKK). Earnings per share is the company's adjusted figure, the basis the brokers forecast. Only two brokers forecast the company, so "the two brokers" means the median of Deutsche Bank (Buy, target DKK 100) and DNB Carnegie (Hold, target DKK 85), not a broad consensus.

#0 The investment case

The case in brief

The shares cost 7.45 times earnings two years ahead, an earnings yield of 13%, and the three concerns that put them there are each clearing on a dated event. The three concerns are net debt of 3.0 times EBITDA, a suspended buyback and self-inflicted supply failures in Europe. Profit only has to stay flat for the case to work: the free cash flow then pays a 5.5% dividend and retires about 6% of the shares a year, so earnings per share grows about 7% a year and the owner earns roughly the earnings yield, with any re-rating on top. The objection is that 2026 profit includes DKK 166 million of duty and tariff refunds that will not recur. Flat profit therefore has to be earned in 2027, by a company that missed its opening guidance in three of the last four years.

What drives the case up

  • Cash: about 100% of profit converts to cash, and free cash flow is about 15% of the market value.
  • The repaired balance sheet: net debt falls to about 2.0 times EBITDA, below the 2.5 times ceiling.
  • The buyback: each DKK 100 million a year adds about 1% a year to earnings per share.
  • The price Japan Tobacco paid: 12 times EBITDA for two brands of a group valued at about 6 times.

What could break the case

  • The DKK 166 million of refunds in 2026 profit do not recur in 2027.
  • Volumes fall 3% to 5% a year, and price rises only just cover the fall.
  • Opening guidance was missed in three of the last four years.
  • The shares have fallen 13% to 34% in a results month about once a year.

The scorecard: momentum and the fair multiple score best; the environment and the guidance record score worst.

1

1. The one idea: Scandinavian Tobacco Group is a cash-rich leader in shrinking tobacco niches, so its growth in earnings per share is decided by what it does with the cash.

The company owns the leading brands in niches too small for the cigarette majors: handmade cigars in the United States (about 13% of the market, and 42% to 43% of online sales through its own websites and 15 superstores), machine-rolled cigars in Europe (25.8% of volume) and pipe tobacco (about 90% of the world market). It earns an EBITDA margin of 20% and turns almost all of that profit into cash, because capital spending is only 2% of sales. The niches, however, shrink by 3% to 5% a year in volume and, unlike cigarettes, they are fragmented, so price rises only just cover the lost volume.

Three conclusions follow. The company's competitive position is scale inside small categories, not pricing power. The main risk is that volume falls faster than price rises and cost savings can cover, on a fixed cost base. And because profit is flat at best, the use of the cash decides the growth in earnings per share.

2

2. The change: the balance sheet and the cost base have changed; demand has not.

Net debt reached 3.0 times EBITDA at the end of 2025, which forced a 47% dividend cut and stopped the buybacks. The company then sold two German fine-cut tobacco brands, BREAK and Moro (6% of EBITDA), to Japan Tobacco for DKK 1.3 billion. The price was about 12 times EBITDA, twice the multiple the whole group trades on, and the proceeds take net debt to about 2.0 times EBITDA at the end of 2026, against the company's ceiling of 2.5 times. Two cost programmes are worth DKK 350 million before reinvestment, about 19% of EBITDA: the Mac Baren integration (DKK 150 million by 2027) and the Focus2030 simplification onto one SAP system (DKK 200 million over two years). The supply failures that lost European market share (the SAP roll-out in 2025 and a tobacco leaf defect in the Signature brand in 2026) are fixed, and the last SAP stage is due in early 2027.

Four forces work against the change. The volume decline continues. The DKK 166 million of duty and tariff refunds in 2026 (9% of EBITDA) will not recur. The brand sale removes about DKK 107 million of EBITDA a year. And most of the forecasters cited in the Risks report expect the dollar (47% of sales, unhedged) to weaken over the next two years. There is no demand tailwind.

3

3. How the change reaches the financials: through the lines below EBITDA, not through sales.

Sales fall about 1% in 2027 and are flat after that. EBITDA stays near DKK 1.8 billion from 2026 to 2028, because about DKK 190 million of savings and one-off recoveries in 2027 fill most of the DKK 246 million gap left by the refunds and the sold brands. Interest falls from about DKK 215 million to DKK 165 million as debt falls. Free cash flow of DKK 1.0 to 1.1 billion a year after leases, about 15% of the market value of DKK 6.7 billion, pays the dividend and leaves about DKK 650 million a year, of which I assume DKK 400 million buys back shares.

On those assumptions my earnings per share is 10.9 in 2026, 10.9 in 2027, 11.9 in 2028 and 13.0 in 2029, against the two brokers' 10.85, 11.20, 11.50 and 12.00. I am 3% below the two brokers for 2027, because I give more weight to the lost refunds. I am 4% above them for 2028 wholly because of the share count: one broker includes a single DKK 0.5 billion buyback and the other includes none. Guidance for 2027 arrives on 3-Mar-27 and is likely to be set cautiously. The brokers' operating forecasts therefore have little room to rise, but their per-share forecasts rise when a buyback is announced, and the market's narrative can move from "a shrinking business with a stretched balance sheet" to "a share that pays out a 13% earnings yield".

4

4. The foundation: the business is of medium quality at best but strong in cash, and the case leans on the cash.

Return on invested capital is 8%, the EBITDA margin has fallen from 27% in 2021 to 20%, and the first guidance of the year was missed in 2022, 2023 and 2025. The research rates the chief executive a strong allocator of capital and a weak operator, and the damage in Europe was self-inflicted. The cash record supports the case: about 100% of profit converted to cash, almost DKK 6 billion returned to shareholders in five years, 21% of the shares retired since 2020, and the full DKK 250 million of savings delivered from the Agio integration.

The case therefore rests on strengths the company has shown (cash generation, cost removal and capital return). It needs the strength the company has not shown (reliable operations) only to hold steady, and that need is exactly where the case is fragile.

5

5. The setup: a set of causes for concern clearing, with a mechanical buyback leg added.

The case fits best the setup "Major CfC Clearing in MQ non-cyclical or better business on Q1 multiple, leading to reversion to normal", in which CfC means causes for concern, MQ means medium-quality and Q1 means a first-quartile multiple. Present in this case: three causes for concern clearing on dated events, in a largely non-cyclical business. Missing or weak: the multiple is no longer in the first quartile (it is at the 33rd percentile of ten years, after a 44% rise from the 52-week low of DKK 59.5); "medium quality" is generous; and "normal" means today's profit with a normal payout, not a return to the earnings per share of 14 to 16 seen in 2021 to 2024. The buyback adds a second, mechanical leg that resembles the "Mechanical EPS Upgrader" setup, without that setup's acquisitions.

6

6. The reward and the skew: about 19% weighted over 18 months, skewed upwards in size but not in odds.

If the case plays out (my base case, 50% probability), the shares return about 32% over 18 months: earnings per share two years ahead rises 13%, the multiple rises 6% to its ten-year median of 7.9 times, and two dividends add 11%. If the company also delivers 2027 cleanly and the multiple reaches the guideline fair multiple of 8.87 times (better case, 15%), the return is about 60%. If the 2027 profit base disappoints and no meaningful buyback follows (worse case, 35%), forward earnings per share falls to about 9.6, the multiple falls to 6.6 times, and the return is about (16)%. Weighted by probability, the return is about 19% over 18 months.

The outcomes are skewed upwards in size, but the odds are not unusual, because operating forecasts are as likely to fall as to rise. The shares have already shown the downside: they fell 34% in March 2026, the month of the 2025 results, the lower guidance and the dividend cut.

7

7. What has to be true, and when Richard can know.

Two of the three tests fall on one day, 3-Mar-27; Europe is tested at the first-quarter and half-year results.

3-Mar-27full-year results

3-Mar-27, full-year results: the fourth quarter holds without the timing help. Richard would see fourth-quarter EBITDA before special items near DKK 390 to 400 million (including the last DKK 50 million of refunds), full-year earnings per share near 10.9, net debt near 2.0 times EBITDA, and 2027 guidance whose mid-point supports earnings per share of about 11 with no refunds in it.

3-Mar-27, same announcement: the board restarts the buyback at DKK 0.5 billion or more. Management has said the buyback decision comes with the annual report.

May and late Aug 2027first-quarter and half-year results

First-quarter results (May 2027) and half-year results (late August 2027): Europe holds. Richard would see the company's volume share of European machine-rolled cigars stop falling from 25.8%, the last SAP stage pass without stock-outs, handmade cigars still growing, and first-half EBITDA before special items of about DKK 810 million, against DKK 835 million a year earlier, which included DKK 79 million of refunds.

The five judgements that move the value of the shares most

The multiple and the buyback move the value of the shares most; a 5% fall in the dollar moves it least.

Judgement 1: the board restarts the buyback and repeats it (my base case: DKK 400 million a year from March 2027).

  • DKK 100 million of buyback buys about 1.14 million shares at DKK 88, which is 1.45% of the 78.7 million shares in issue, so earnings per share rises 1.45%.
  • The interest forgone on that DKK 100 million is DKK 100 million x 4.7% x (1 less 23.5% tax) = DKK 3.6 million, or 0.4% of net income. The net gain is therefore about 1% of earnings per share a year for each DKK 100 million a year of buyback.
  • At DKK 400 million a year, earnings per share in 2029 is 13.0. With no buyback, 2029 earnings per share is 11.7, 10% lower. With all the spare cash (DKK 650 million a year), 2029 earnings per share is about 13.8, 6% higher.
  • The brand sale shows why the buyback matters. The sale of BREAK and Moro removes about DKK 82 million of net income, while repaying debt with the DKK 1.0 billion of proceeds saves only DKK 36 million, so the sale alone lowers earnings per share by about 5%. A DKK 0.5 billion buyback brings earnings per share back to its level before the sale. The buyback is what makes the sale worth doing per share; it is not a bonus on top.

Judgement 2: the EBITDA margin holds near 20% once the refunds stop.

  • The refunds are worth DKK 166 million x (1 less 23.5% tax) / 78.7 million shares = DKK 1.6 of the DKK 10.9 earned per share in 2026, or 15%. The sold brands remove a further DKK 0.8 a share in 2027. Together, DKK 2.4 a share has to be replaced in 2027.
  • My replacements, per share: cost savings of DKK 120 million (1.2); no repeat of the Signature write-down, DKK 35 million (0.35); own distribution in Norway and Canada, DKK 25 million (0.25); contract manufacturing, DKK 10 million (0.10); lower interest, DKK 40 million (0.40); fewer shares (0.27); and weaker underlying trading, DKK 20 million ((0.20)). The replacements total DKK 2.4 a share, which is why my 2027 earnings per share is flat at 10.9.
  • If the savings deliver only half (DKK 60 million less), the 2027 margin is 19.4% and 2027 earnings per share is 10.3, 5% lower. Each 0.5 point of margin is DKK 44 million of EBITDA and DKK 0.44 a share, or 4% of earnings per share.

Judgement 3: the company's European machine-rolled cigar volume stabilises.

  • 2 points of group volume is about DKK 176 million of sales. On a fixed cost base, about half of that lost sales value drops to profit: DKK 92 million of EBITDA, DKK 70 million after tax, DKK 0.89 a share, or 8% of earnings per share.
  • The European market declines 3% to 5% a year, and the company lost 2.1 points of market share in two years. A further year of share loss on top of the market decline would cost 4% to 8% of earnings per share.

Judgement 4: the dollar does not fall far.

  • A 5% fall in the dollar removes about DKK 225 million of sales and DKK 46 million of EBITDA, which is DKK 0.45 a share, or 4% of earnings per share. The company does not hedge its currency exposure.
  • Nordea forecasts the euro at 1.14 dollars in the second half of 2027 and at 1.20 dollars by the end of 2028. My forecasts hold the currency flat, because the files do not give today's exchange rate.

Judgement 5: the multiple the market pays for buyback-led growth.

  • One turn of the price-to-earnings multiple is worth DKK 11.5 a share, 13% of the share price. On today's forward earnings per share of 11.46, the range from the tenth-percentile multiple (6.6 times) to the guideline fair multiple (8.87 times) is a share price of DKK 76 to DKK 102.

#1 Operating environment

Conclusion

The operating environment offers no tailwind and no new headwind, so it neither makes nor breaks the case. The market gives no growth, so the case has to work with flat sales.

Bearing on the case: the absence of a tailwind leaves step 2 resting wholly on the internal change, and it is the reason step 3 runs through cash rather than sales.

Evidence. The external forces divide into a steady set of headwinds and a smaller set of offsets.

Headwinds

  • Cigar and smoking tobacco volumes fall 3% to 5% a year, and DNB Carnegie judges that price rises "barely" cover the fall.
  • Consumers are trading down in Europe and the United States.
  • The company's volume share of European machine-rolled cigars fell from 27.9% in 2024 to 25.8% in the first nine months of 2026.
  • Germany raises tobacco excise from January 2027, lifting retail prices by 12% to 14%.
  • The revision of the European Tobacco Products Directive, expected between 2028 and 2030, targets packaging, flavours and online sales.
  • The nicotine pouch market in Sweden, Denmark and the United Kingdom grew 19% by volume in the first nine months of 2026, but British American Tobacco holds 49% to 69% of those markets, and DNB Carnegie calls the category "barely profitable" for a small maker.

Offsets

  • United States regulation is benign: a court vacated the federal regulation of premium cigars in 2023.
  • The company's handmade cigar sales grew 4% in a slightly falling market.
  • Sweden won a deferral of the European tax on nicotine pouches.

Inference. The environment is a steady headwind that is neither improving nor worsening. The one clear change is the company's own: it sold its German fine-cut brands, its position most exposed to the German excise rise, three months before the rise and at 12 times EBITDA.

Where I differ from the market. The market read third-quarter organic growth of 2.1% as stabilisation. Organic growth over the nine months was only 0.5%, and about (0.5)% without the DKK 70 million of shipments pulled forward from the fourth quarter. I read the trend as "no longer getting worse", not as "stable".

Third-quarter revenue grew 3.3% after five quarters of decline, and net debt fell to 2.76 times EBITDA.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Enforcement against illicit vapes and a benign United States could bring volume back. Two successive quarters of positive organic growth in the Europe Branded division, with European market share above 26.5%, would move my view up. A harsh first draft of the European directive in 2027 would move it down.

Score: 29, set by the Rater. The external forces are a steady structural headwind: cigar and pipe volumes fall 3-5% a year with price rises that only just cover them, consumers trade down, the European directive (2028-30) targets packaging, flavours and online sales, and pouches are a BAT-dominated, barely profitable category; benign US regulation and growing handmade cigars only partly offset, and the German excise rise falls on brands now sold (judged on the business as it will be). Consensus sales growth at the 7th percentile is honest, so I place it a little above Imperial Brands' fully combustible decline and close to Greggs' falling volumes.

#2 Internal change forces

Conclusion

The internal change is real, dated and mostly financial: the operating programmes restore profit, and the financial changes add to earnings per share.

Bearing on the case: the internal change is the whole of step 2 and supports step 3, on the condition that the board uses the cash as judgement 1 assumes.

Evidence. Net debt falls from 3.0 times EBITDA in December 2025 to 2.7 times in September 2026 and to about 2.0 times in December 2026, on DKK 1.0 billion of post-tax proceeds from the brand sale. The two cost programmes total DKK 350 million. The company took over its own distribution in Norway in June 2026 and takes over the SAIL brand in Canada in the second quarter of 2027. Special items were DKK 178 million in the first nine months of 2026, and DNB Carnegie estimates about DKK 245 million for the year. Most special items come from the SAP roll-out and the Mac Baren integration, and both end in 2027.

Inference. Three points matter more than the list of changes.

1The brand sale creates value per share only if the cash buys shares (the arithmetic is in judgement 1). The board's buyback decision on 3-Mar-27 completes the sale's logic; it is not a separate event.
2The 2027 cost programmes are needed for profit to stand still. The savings replace the refunds and the sold brands. They are not a source of upgrades.
3Reported earnings catch up with adjusted earnings. Reported earnings per share was 8.50 in 2025, against 10.80 adjusted. As special items fall from about DKK 245 million to about DKK 70 million by 2028, reported earnings per share rises by about DKK 1.8 with no change in adjusted earnings per share, and cash rises with it.

Where I differ from the market. Deutsche Bank expects delivery of the Focus2030 programme to re-rate the shares; DNB Carnegie doubts the delivery. My view sits between the two. The programmes will probably be delivered, because cost removal is what this management does well, but they buy stability, and the re-rating has to come from the cash.

Counter-case. Change programmes are where this company has failed before. The SAP roll-out caused the stock-outs of 2025, the previous strategy missed its margin aims, and the last SAP stage in early 2027 overlaps the move of Mac Baren production to Holstebro, due by summer 2027.

What would change my view. A first half of 2027 that shows the savings in the margin with no new disruption would raise my confidence. A new supply problem would lower it sharply, because it would be the third in three years.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. Real, funded and dated self-help: the BREAK/Moro sale at about 12x EBITDA (twice the group's multiple) takes debt from 3.0x to about 2.0x, DKK 350m of cost programmes (about 19% of EBITDA), own distribution in Norway and Canada and special items falling, with a buyback likely to follow; but the operating programmes only replace the lost refunds and sold brands, and two self-inflicted supply failures with a third risk where the last SAP stage overlaps the Mac Baren move make this complete repair-only self-help on a mature business, net of real operational problems. It sits just below Odfjell's acquisition-plus-deleveraging and above Shell's incremental self-help, because the disposal price and deleveraging are proportionately larger.

#3 Value chain, business model, financial profile and management

Conclusion

Scandinavian Tobacco Group is a medium-quality niche leader with below-average returns, above-average cash conversion, and a management better at allocating capital than at running operations.

Bearing on the case: the foundation supports step 4 only in part. It is good enough for a case built on cash, and too weak for a case built on profit growth.

Value chain. Leaf growers are weak (more than 5,000 suppliers in over 40 countries), and retail buyers are strong and consolidating. The company's answer in the United States is to own the route to the consumer: about 55% of handmade cigars are sold online, the company has 42% to 43% of those online sales, and its superstores earn more than 15% on capital after three years.

Financial profile. Divisional EBITDA margins run from 31% in North America Branded to 13% in North America Online and Retail. The group margin of 20% compares with 43% at Imperial Brands and 47% at British American Tobacco. Working capital is 47% of sales, because tobacco is held for 233 days.

Management and owners. The chief executive has led the company since 2015, after a career in the supply chain, and is candid about it ("not a growth machine"). Insiders own 0.72% of the shares, and neither the chief executive nor the finance chief has bought shares. The last two long-term incentive cycles paid out 15% and nothing. Two foundations own over 40% of the shares, and Parvus holds 5%.

Consensus has Europe Branded shrinking from DKK 3.3 billion in 2025 to 2.6 billion in 2028, after the brand sale, while North America Online & Retail grows.

Inference. The company's barriers to entry are real (brands, scale in leaf buying and the online customer base), but they protect a shrinking pool and do not widen on their own. The company's goals are modest rather than stretching: low-single-digit growth in operating profit and a return on invested capital above 11% by 2030.

Where I differ from the market. The brokers' valuation story is a 53% discount to tobacco peers. The fair comparison is Imperial Brands, another shrinking cash business that grows per share through buybacks. Imperial trades on 6.9 times earnings with twice the margin, stronger pricing and growth in earnings per share of 7% to 9%. Against that analogue, Scandinavian Tobacco Group's 7.4 times is not a discount. The better evidence of hidden value is the price Japan Tobacco paid: 12 times EBITDA for brands inside a group valued at about 6 times.

Against Imperial Brands, the closest analogue, the shares are not at a discount; the price Japan Tobacco paid is the better sign of hidden value.

Counter-case. The five-year record understates the business, because 2021 to 2025 combined a pandemic boom and bust in handmade cigars with a one-off systems change. What would change my view: return on invested capital rising towards 10% by 2028, with a stable European market share.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. Real niche leadership (about 90% of pipe tobacco, 42-43% of US online handmade cigars with own superstores, 25.8% of European machine-rolled cigars) protects shrinking, fragmented pools where price only just covers volume, against strong retailers; management is a good capital allocator but a weak operator with modest goals. The figures confirm an ordinary-to-weak profile: ROIC 5.2% (39th percentile; 8% on the memo's basis, near the cost of capital), EBITDA margin at the median but down from 27% to 20% (margin change 13th percentile), and the 19th-percentile cash conversion is a 2025 working-capital and special-items distortion against a long record near 100%; low predictability keeps it below IMCD's distribution moat and above CVS Group.

#4 Guidance and delivery record

Conclusion

Current guidance is safe for 2026, and the company's record gives no right to assume the same for 2027.

Bearing on the case: the guidance record weakens step 4 and makes 3-Mar-27 the single most important date in step 7.

Evidence. The company missed its opening guidance by (6)% in 2022, (6)% in 2023 and (12)% in 2025, and beat it by 1% in 2024. In 2026 the company raised guidance for the first time in this period: the operating margin before special items to 14.0% to 15.5%, from 13.0% to 14.5%, and earnings per share to 9.5 to 11.5, from 9 to 11. Management's tone is careful. It did not raise guidance after a good first quarter, it said that "one quarter does not change a trend", and the chief executive himself flagged the reversal due in the fourth quarter.

Opening guidance was missed in three of the last four years; 2026 is the first year it was raised.

Inference. Management's words are conservative, but its numbers have not been. Two points follow.

  • The November 2026 raise was not an underlying upgrade. The refunds are worth 1.9 points of margin, and the guidance range rose by only 1.0 point. The files do not say how much of the refunds the March guidance already included, but unless it included most of them, the company's underlying view did not rise.
  • 2026 was the first year with a low opening bar, set straight after the 12% miss of 2025, and the low bar worked. I expect the same approach on 3-Mar-27, which is good for the year and awkward for the day: a 2027 range with a mid-point below the brokers' 11.2 would trim their forecasts at the outset.

My probabilities. The risk of disappointment sits at the start of 2027, not in 2026: I see a 2027 opening range below the two brokers as three times as likely as one above them.

Where I differ from the market. The shares rose 9.5% on the November raise, as if earnings power had risen. I think the raise came mostly from the refunds.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Management may have learnt from the misses, and its guidance may now be a floor. A 2027 range that is met or raised at the half year, with no one-off gains, would be the first evidence of that change.

Score: 36, set by the Rater. Opening guidance was missed by 6% in 2022, 6% in 2023 and 12% in 2025 and beaten by 1% only in 2024; 2026 brought the first raise, from a deliberately low bar, but the 1.0-point margin raise is smaller than the 1.9 points of refunds, so the underlying view hardly rose, and 2027 opening guidance is more likely below the brokers than above (45% vs 15%). One refund-flattered raise does not repair three misses in four years, so it sits just below Hexatronic and above Indutrade.

#5 Earnings gearing

Conclusion

Sales growth cannot lead to outsized profit growth here, because there is no sales growth; cash leads to outsized growth in earnings per share instead.

Bearing on the case: the gearing analysis supports step 3 and explains why the share count, not the margin, is judgement 1.

Evidence and inference. The company's pricing power is weak. Operating leverage exists but works against the company, because volumes fall (judgement 3). The gearing that works in the company's favour sits in two places.

  • Cost removal: DKK 350 million of cost programmes, against EBITDA of DKK 1.8 billion.
  • The share count, helped by the low multiple: at 7.5 times earnings, a DKK 400 million buyback retires shares that carry about DKK 53 million of yearly earnings. The lower the multiple stays, the more each krone of buyback adds, so a slow re-rating is not wasted time for a holder.

The two loops. The helpful loop runs from cash to fewer shares, to higher earnings and dividends per share, to more cash per share. The harmful loop, seen in Europe from 2024 to 2026, runs from falling volume to fixed costs spread over less, to price rises that compensate, to consumers trading down, to lost market share.

The cash loop compounds per-share value; the volume loop, seen in Europe in 2024 to 2026, erodes share.

The helpful loop

Where I differ from the market. There is no real difference: both brokers model flat sales and rising earnings per share. I put more of the growth in earnings per share into the share count, and less into the margin, than Deutsche Bank does.

Counter-case. If the company regained European market share towards its aim of 29% by 2030, operating leverage would turn positive; the files do not let me size the profit effect of a point of European share. What would change my view: a year of positive volume in machine-rolled cigars.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. The structure has weak pricing power (price only covers volume decline) and a fixed cost base where about half of lost sales drops to EBITDA, so operating leverage is real but currently works against profit; the gears that help are cost-out scope (DKK 350m, about 19% of EBITDA) and the share count, where a buyback at about 7.5x earnings turns flat profit into about 7% EPS growth on debt falling to 2.0x. That is leverage asymmetric with no pricing power behind it, offset by unusually large cost-out and cash-to-shares scope, so a little below the ordinary mix.

The tests I applied before setting these forecasts.

  • Does the company's delivery make the change plausible? Flat profit is supported by the record so far: excluding refunds and other income, EBITDA for the first nine months of 2026 was DKK 1,329 million, against DKK 1,298 million a year earlier. The thesis relies on strengths the company has shown (cash, cost removal and buybacks) and on one it has not shown (a year without an operating accident).
  • How wide is the range of outcomes? The range is wide for a consumer staple: 2027 earnings per share could land between about 9.5 and 12, with the risk skewed down in the operating lines and up in the share count.
  • Guidance is tested in topic #4, and the brokers' forecasts in topic #7.

Growth against the past. Operating profit does not grow at a double-digit rate on any reading, and I assume the company falls short of its own aim of low-single-digit growth, as it did under the previous strategy. Earnings per share grows about 7% a year from 2026 to 2030, or about 8% a year if all the spare cash buys shares, against a fall of about (8)% a year from 2021 to 2025. Margins stay below the past: about 20%, against 22% to 27% in 2019 to 2024.

The EBITDA margin fell from 26.7% in 2021 to 19.2% in 2025 and net interest rose from DKK 97 million to DKK 256 million, while the share count fell from 99.7 to 78.7 million.

#7 Scope for upgrades not yet in guidance or the brokers' forecasts

Conclusion

There is scope for upgrades to the brokers' per-share forecasts on a dated event, the buyback decision, and little scope for upgrades to their operating forecasts.

Bearing on the case: the scope for upgrades supports the last link of step 3 for earnings per share and leaves that link open for profit.

What is left to upgrade.

  • The buyback is the only clear source of upgrades. About half of one DKK 0.5 billion programme is already in the two brokers' median. An announcement of DKK 0.5 billion adds about 5% to 6% to Deutsche Bank's 2028 earnings per share, and therefore about 3% to the median, and a repeated programme adds about 4% a year after that. I put the chance of an announcement of at least DKK 0.5 billion on 3-Mar-27 at about 65%. Debt will be below the ceiling, and buybacks are the company's stated way of returning excess cash, but management wants to "assess the outer-year outlook" first and may prefer to keep room for acquisitions.
  • More than my DKK 400 million a year is affordable. Even at DKK 400 million a year, net debt falls to 1.4 times EBITDA by 2030, so about DKK 250 to 300 million a year is unallocated in my numbers.
  • My numbers contain no operating upgrades. Possible sources that nobody forecasts are Mac Baren savings arriving early, making nicotine pouches in-house (bought-in production caps their gross margin at 25% to 30%) and further refunds. The files do not let me size them.
  • Guidance for 2026 has no upgrade left: the earnings per share range of 9.5 to 11.5 should land near 10.9.

The two brokers see EBITDA near DKK 1.8 billion through 2028 and earnings per share rising to 11.50.

With only two brokers, one Buy and one Hold, one revision is the whole of the net breadth.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The two brokers may still be anchored on three bad years and may under-forecast the cost programmes. A clean fourth quarter and first-quarter 2027 EBITDA above DKK 305 million would show that.

With revenue growth about nil, the per-share raise is large against the growth rate but rests on one board decision, so scope is slightly negative-to-flat, between Tele2's limited scope and IMCD's.

#8 Current momentum

Conclusion

Momentum is positive and the best in a weak sector, but it is not yet proven beyond one quarter flattered by refunds.

Bearing on the case: momentum supports step 3 modestly, and it shows that the market has already taken part of the reward in step 6.

Evidence (dashboard, 23-Nov-26). The pinned ratings are C for technical momentum, C for sell-side earnings momentum and B for valuation; thematic fit is A, on the environment only. One of the two brokers rates the shares Buy. The 200-day moving average has risen in only 2 of the last 12 months, and the share price is 17% above that average. Peers. Scandinavian Tobacco Group has the best revision score in the dashboard's tobacco sector: 11, against (13) for Imperial Brands, (1) for British American Tobacco and (4) for Haypp. The momentum ratings of the two large peers are D or F, and Japan Tobacco has just written off its Russian business and cut its dividend.

Inference. The momentum is good but young: it rests on one quarter, fed by refunds and shipment timing, in a sector where momentum is otherwise poor. The price trend is a recovery inside a twelve-month range, not yet a new trend.

Where I differ from the market. I see no real difference on the facts. I give the revision momentum less weight than its rating suggests, because the fourth quarter of 2026 will show EBITDA lower than a year earlier even if everything goes to plan.

Counter-case and what would change my view. A buyback and clean 2027 guidance would give the momentum a second leg. A fourth-quarter reversal larger than the company flagged would end it.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. Both measures positive and neither strongly negative gives B: guidance raised on 11-Nov-26, 2027 EPS forecasts up 14% in three months, targets up 20-22% and the best revision score in a weak tobacco sector. I place it low in the band because the upgrades were fed by one-off refunds, 2027 forecasts are still 6% below a year ago, the brokers are split one Buy one Hold, and the 200-day average has barely turned (technical momentum C on the dashboard).

#9 Riskiness and simplicity

Conclusion

The case is simple and carries little debt, but it has one concentrated fragility and a record of sharp falls on results days.

Bearing on the case: the risk profile sets the 35% weight on the worse case in step 6 and explains why the odds are ordinary.

Simplicity. The case rests on three drivers (flat profit, falling interest and fewer shares), and Richard can track all three each quarter.

Fragility. The case's fragility is concentrated in one place and on one date: the 2027 profit base, which the company shows on 3-Mar-27.

The risks, grouped by how they arrive.

  • Sudden and material: sharp falls on results days. The month-end share price fell (20)% in August 2022, (13)% in May 2023, (14)% in May 2024 and (34)% in March 2026, each time in a month of results or new guidance. That record amounts to about one such fall a year.
  • Trackable: European market share, the size of special items and net debt. These three measures give warning before the profit line does.
  • Currency: the company's dollar exposure is unhedged, unlike that of any named peer (judgement 4).
  • Cyclical: handmade cigars are a discretionary purchase. They are 35% of sales on the annual report's product split; the brokers say about 45%, a difference the files do not explain. The group margin fell from 27% to 19% as the pandemic boom in handmade cigars reversed.
  • Rulings by governments and courts, the sector's precedent: tobacco shocks arrive by ruling, not by trend. This autumn Japan Tobacco lost control of its Russian business, and Haypp closed a Swedish website after a court ruling. For Scandinavian Tobacco Group the relevant rulings are the European directive (2028 to 2030), rules on flavours, and an end to the United States embargo on Cuba. An end to the embargo is unlikely and cannot be tracked, but it would hit the most profitable division.
  • Small items: an unprovisioned Belgian excise claim of EUR 7 to 9 million, and the Cohiba trademark case, which has run since 1997.

Against the investment environment. The weekly environment note is Overweight consumer staples and tobacco, but Double Underweight fragile small companies. Scandinavian Tobacco Group is small: about DKK 6.7 billion of market value, with USD 2 to 4 million of shares traded a day. The case answers balance-sheet fragility with evidence (net debt of 2.0 times EBITDA) but does not answer earnings fragility. The return does not need a lower discount rate.

Where I differ from the market. The Risks report rates the chance of missing earnings expectations as medium. I agree with that level and add that the risk is bunched on one date.

What would change my view. Two results days without a reset of expectations would lower my 35% weight on the worse case.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. The case is simple (flat profit, falling interest, fewer shares) and trackable, debt falls to about 2.0x, and most demand is non-cyclical; but the memo's 2027 EPS cone is about 9.5-12 around 10.9 (about (13)%/+10%, skewed down operationally), the fragility is bunched on one date, the shares have fallen 13-34% in a results month about once a year, 47% of sales are in unhedged dollars, handmade cigars (35-45% of sales) are discretionary, and tobacco risk arrives by ruling. That is a wider-range simple case like IMCD's (three years of downgrades, unhedged FX) with less leverage but sharper results-day falls, so just below IMCD and above Rexel.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion

The stock is turning up, on the edge of broadening, and it has to earn broadening on 3-Mar-27.

Bearing on the case: the lifecycle reading supports step 5 (causes for concern clearing) and argues for the more cautious multiple in step 6.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule puts the starting phase at Broadening. The evidence divides as follows.

For Broadening

  • The first guidance raise in years.
  • Three to six months of rising forecasts.
  • A 44% rise in the share price from the low.
  • One broker upgraded to Buy in July.

Against Broadening

  • Forecasts are still 6% to 12% below a year ago.
  • The 200-day moving average has barely turned.
  • The two brokers are split.
  • The upgrades so far have one source, the refunds.

I place the stock one phase earlier than the dashboard's rule: turning up, with broadening to be earned on 3-Mar-27.

For Scandinavian Tobacco Group the second reason (the buyback) and the third (a clean 2027 profit base) are both due on the same day, 3-Mar-27. The stock is not stalling: the change is too recent, and the cash events are still ahead.

Where I differ. I place the stock one phase earlier than the dashboard's rule. The market, with one Buy and one Hold, is undecided between the two readings.

An early but unconfirmed, partly one-off turn sits just below Nexans and above Greggs' Bottoming/early Turning.

#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion

The guideline fair multiple of 8.87 times is reachable if 2027 is clean, but I would not count on it inside 18 months; my central multiple is 7.9 times.

Bearing on the case: the fair multiple sets the upper end of step 6, and it is the reason my base case uses a smaller re-rating than the guideline.

The guideline. The guideline fair multiple is 8.87 times earnings two years ahead, the 80th percentile of the stock's ten-year range, set for the Broadening phase. It is 19% above today's 7.45 times.

My view: 8.87 times is fair as a three-year ceiling and generous for 18 months.

  • History since late 2018. In the 96 months since November 2018, the month-end multiple has been at or above 8.7 times in only 12 months, in short peaks (around the start of 2019, in 2020, in early and late 2021, in February 2022 and in February 2026), and it fell back after each peak. It has been at or above the guideline itself in only three months. The five-year median is 7.26 times, and today's multiple is already at the 64th percentile of five years.
  • The kind of growth. The market capitalises buyback-led growth in a shrinking business at a low multiple: Imperial Brands trades on 6.9 times.
  • The phase. On my reading the stock is turning up, a phase that calls for a multiple lower in the range than Broadening does.
  • I therefore use 7.9 times, the ten-year median, as the central multiple for 18 months, and 8.87 times only if the company delivers 2027 with no one-off gains.

Where I differ from the market. Deutsche Bank's target of DKK 100 implies about 8.7 times today's forward earnings per share, close to the guideline. DNB Carnegie's target of DKK 85 implies 7.4 times, no re-rating. My 7.9 times sits between the two.

Counter-case. At 8.87 times, the earnings yield is still 11%. If the market comes to trust a repeated buyback, 8.87 times is not expensive, and the multiples of 2016 to 2018 show what that trust once paid.

What would change my view. A first half of 2027 delivered with no one-off gains would move my central multiple up to the guideline.

Score: 75, set by the Rater. Cheap on one measure and neutral on the other gives B; I place it at the floor because the own-range reading sits exactly on the cheap line, and part of the cheapness is deserved: buyback-led growth in a shrinking business is capitalised low, the history includes years of EPS of 14-16, and a stock that is only turning up warrants a multiple below its range median rather than the guideline 8.87x.

#12 Total shareholder return

Conclusion

The weighted return is about 19% over 18 months; over three years it is about 14% to 16% a year without the guideline multiple and about 20% a year with it.

Bearing on the case: the return analysis is step 6, and it shows that the reward comes from cash and the risk comes from the profit base.

The return at the guideline fair multiple, on my forecasts.

  • Over 18 months (to May 2028): about 50%. Earnings per share two years ahead rises from 11.46 (the brokers' figure the price reflects today) to 13.4 on my forecasts for the twelve months to May 2030, a gain of 17%. The multiple rises from 7.45 to 8.87 times, a gain of 19%. The share price becomes 8.87 x 13.4 = DKK 119, up 39%. Dividends of 4.70 + 4.90 = DKK 9.6 add 11% of today's price. The total return is about 50%.
  • Over three years (to November 2029): about 72%, or 20% a year. Forward earnings per share reaches about 14.9, assuming 2031 continues at about 15, a gain of 30%. The multiple gain is 19%, and the share price becomes DKK 132. Dividends of 4.70 + 4.90 + 5.10 = DKK 14.7 add 17%.

My own estimate. I treat the full guideline multiple inside 18 months as the better case, not the base case.

  • The weighted figure: 15% x 60% + 50% x 32% + 35% x (16)% = 9 + 16 less 6 = 19% over 18 months.
  • Three years on my central multiple of 7.9 times: a share price of DKK 118 plus DKK 14.7 of dividends, about 55%, or 16% a year. At an unchanged 7.45 times, the return is about 47%, or 14% a year.

What drives the return. In the base case the dividend gives 11 percentage points, earnings per share 13 points and the multiple 6 points. None of the growth in earnings per share is profit growth: it comes from fewer shares, lower interest and the brokers moving to that lower share count. The return is therefore close to the earnings yield being handed over to shareholders, and it holds only while profit holds. The worse case shows the other side: the same gearing that turns flat profit into 7% growth in earnings per share turns a 10% fall in profit into a reset of both earnings and the multiple.

Where I differ from the market. My base case implies a share price of about DKK 97 after twelve months, between the brokers' twelve-month targets of DKK 85 and DKK 100. DNB Carnegie's bull and bear values of DKK 120 and DKK 60 match my better and worse cases closely, so any disagreement with DNB Carnegie is on the weights, not on the range.

What would change my view. The 3-Mar-27 announcement moves the weights directly. With a buyback and 2027 guidance in line with the brokers, I would move about 15 points of probability from the worse case to the base case.

#13 Summary conclusion

Scandinavian Tobacco Group is a medium-quality, shrinking and very cash-generative niche leader whose balance sheet has just been repaired. The investment case is real and simple: a 13% earnings yield that is about to be paid out again, with 3-Mar-27 as the day the company shows both its 2027 profit base and its payout.

The case is moderately strong on reward (about 19% weighted over 18 months, and 32% in the base case), moderate on certainty (a 35% chance of a loss of about 16%), and unusually easy to check. The upward skew is in the size of the outcomes and in the per-share forecasts, not in the operating forecasts. The evidence that would make the case stronger is 2027 profit holding without refunds, and nothing in the files shows that yet.

What to watch, in order.

  1. 3-Mar-27:fourth-quarter EBITDA before special items (about DKK 390 to 400 million), net debt (about 2.0 times EBITDA), and the mid-point of 2027 guidance against the brokers' 11.2.
  2. 3-Mar-27:the buyback, its size (DKK 0.5 billion or more) and whether the company frames it as yearly.
  3. Early 2027:the last SAP stage and the move of the Mac Baren factory passing without stock-outs.
  4. May and late August 2027:the company's share of European machine-rolled cigars against 25.8%; first-half EBITDA before special items against about DKK 810 million; special items falling.
  5. Through 2027:the dollar, and the first draft of the revised European Tobacco Products Directive.

The four memo ratings

The four memo ratings sit between 40 and 58: a real, dated change on foundations below typical.

47
Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 47, set by the Rater.

The internal change (deleveraging via a 12x disposal, DKK 350m of cost programmes, a likely buyback) is real and dated, but it mostly offsets a structural volume headwind, the loss of DKK 166m of refunds and the sold brands' EBITDA, so forecast profit is flat and EPS grows about 7% only through the share count and interest, below the Universe's median growth; the net change reaching profits is about nil to mildly negative, held off the 40s' lower end by the per-share mechanism.

40
Foundations' Robustness: 40, set by the Rater.

Niche leadership in shrinking pools (dominant pipe tobacco, a US online and superstore route to the consumer), strong long-run cash conversion and modest capital needs are real foundations, but weak pricing power, a margin that fell from 27% to 20% (not the stable, predictable profile that carried CVS Group), returns near the cost of capital and opening guidance missed in three of four years leave them below typical, short of a price-taker earning below its cost of capital.

58
Setups' Fit/Crispness: 58, set by the Rater.

The case fits Major CfC Clearing in MQ non-cyclical business on a Q1 multiple in kind: three causes for concern (debt, the suspended buyback, European supply failures) clear on dated events, the business is largely non-cyclical and the multiple sits about on the first-quartile line; but quality is below medium, 'reversion to normal' means today's flat profit rather than past earnings, the profit base is flattered by refunds and the operating fix is unproven until the last SAP stage passes, and the buyback leg straddles a Mechanical EPS Upgrader, so it sits below Richard's 65-75 for CfC clearing in a mediocre (but more stable) CVS Group.

46
Case Riskiness: 46, set by the Rater.

A simple, trackable three-driver case with debt falling to 2.0x and a low multiple that cushions the downside, but its risks are not paper cuts: a roughly (13)%/+10% EPS cone concentrated on 3-Mar-27, a record of opening-guidance misses and results-month falls of 13-34% about once a year, unhedged dollar exposure, a thin two-broker sell side and illiquid small-cap shares, so slightly below the middle, consistent with topic 9.

Each rating set by the Rater, out of 100.

End notes

Basis of the figures. Money is in Danish kroner. Earnings per share is the company's adjusted figure, before special items and after all depreciation and amortisation, which is the basis the two brokers forecast. Reported basic earnings per share was 8.50 in 2025.

The range of years behind the multiple's percentiles. The monthly history shows multiples of 11 to 13.7 times from November 2016 to October 2018, which does not square with a stated 90th percentile of 9.4 times and only four months removed. The percentile range therefore appears to leave out the years after the listing. For today's business, the range without those years is the right one to use.

The model's horizons and the template's split of the return. The model's two horizons are its fixed columns after the last reported period, so they end on 31-Mar-28 and 30-Sep-29, not 18 months and three years from today. The template's own split (TSR Dupont sheet, rows 46 and 47) measures the same return on trailing twelve-month earnings and the trailing multiple: at the 18-month column, +83.1% from the multiple and (23.1)% from earnings; at the three-year column, +74.6% from the multiple and (10.8)% from earnings. That split reads differently when earnings over the next twelve months are flat or falling, so the split shown in topic #12 is the one to use.
